title: SYSK Selects: How the Black Death Worked
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on the Black Death (1346-1353 pandemic). Josh introduces it as his pick. The hosts cover the Little Ice Age and a Tufts-linked study of stomata counts suggesting population collapse, the disease's gruesome symptoms, the origins at Kaffa (Genoa's trading post in Crimea, modern Ukraine) via the catapulted corpses story, its spread across Europe, the mistranslation of "big death" into "black death," the Paris medical faculty's planetary-alignment explanation (miasma), fire and glass-window precautions, Venice's quarantine origin, the flagellants and the persecution of Jews, social and economic effects, the emergence of modern science and the danse macabre art. They then discuss the bubonic plague (Yersinia pestis) identification from the third pandemic, doubts about whether bubonic plague caused the Black Death, alternative theories (hemorrhagic fever, anthrax, extinct disease), and a listener mail about a listener's family connection to the mob.

segments.title: Selects intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode on the Black Death, then the hosts open with banter.

segments.title: Little Ice Age and stomata study
segments.summary: Chuck describes a 2006 study from the University of Tokyo?

segments.title: Death toll and symptoms
segments.summary: The hosts describe the scale of the Black Death, roughly a third of Europe's population dying within a few years, and its gruesome symptoms including buboes, purple splotches called God's tokens, fevers, and vomiting blood.

segments.title: Origins at Kaffa and spread to Europe
segments.summary: The disease began in Central Asia and China, and was blamed on the Genoese, who fled Kaffa after Tartar forces flung infected corpses over the walls. The plague then spread to Sicily and by two routes across Europe.

segments.title: Name origin and miasma explanation
segments.summary: The name Black Death came from a mistranslation of the original term, the big death or great mortality. The Paris College of Physicians blamed a planetary alignment producing a fog of death, or miasma, and recommended fire and glass windows.

segments.title: Quarantine and other medieval precautions
segments.summary: Venice began isolating ships, first for thirty days and then for forty, which is the origin of the word quarantine. Other advice included avoiding bathing and intimacy, and not sleeping during the day.

segments.title: Flagellants and persecution of Jews
segments.summary: The flagellants whipped themselves across Europe believing the plague was God's punishment. They killed Jews, who were blamed for poisoning water, with mass burnings such as in Strasbourg, and the Pope denounced them in 1349.

segments.title: Social, economic and scientific effects
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the social collapse, religious doubt, economic effects from labor shortages, the rise of modern science and medicine, and the danse macabre art movement.

segments.title: Bubonic plague theory and alternatives
segments.summary: Bubonic plague was identified in the third pandemic by Yersin and Kitasato, and was long assumed to be the Black Death. The hosts note discrepancies in symptoms, rat die-offs and transmission, and discuss alternative theories including a hemorrhagic fever, anthrax, and an extinct disease.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener shares a family story about a relative connected to Lucky Luciano, and the hosts give contact information.
